artists.biography:
Alice in Chains (often abbreviated as AIC) is an American rock band from Seattle, Washington, formed in 1987 by guitarist and vocalist Jerry Cantrell and drummer Sean Kinney, who later recruited bassist Mike Starr and lead vocalist Layne Staley.Starr was replaced by Mike Inez in 1993. William DuVall joined the band in 2006 as co-lead vocalist and rhythm guitarist, replacing Staley, who died in 2002. The band took its name from Staley's previous group, the glam metal band Alice N' Chains.

Often associated with grunge music, Alice in Chains' sound incorporates heavy metal elements. The band is known for its distinctive vocal style, which often included the harmonized vocals between Staley and Cantrell (and later Cantrell and DuVall). Cantrell started to sing lead vocals on the 1992 acoustic EP Sap, and his role continued to grow in the following albums, making Alice in Chains a two-vocal band.

Alice in Chains rose to international fame as part of the grunge movement of the early 1990s, along with other Seattle bands such as Nirvana, Pearl Jam, and Soundgarden. They achieved success during the era with the albums Facelift (1990), Dirt (1992), Alice in Chains (1995), as well as the EP Jar of Flies (1994). Although never officially disbanding, Alice in Chains was plagued by extended inactivity from 1996 onward, due to Staley's substance abuse, which resulted in his death in 2002. The band toured in 2006, with DuVall taking over as lead vocalist full-time. The new line-up have released the albums Black Gives Way to Blue (2009), The Devil Put Dinosaurs Here (2013), and Rainier Fog (2018).

Alice in Chains have sold over 30 million records worldwide, and over 14 million records in the US alone. The band has had 18 Top 10 songs on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Tracks chart, 5 No. 1 hits, and received 11 Grammy Award nominations. The band was ranked number 34 on VH1's 100 Greatest Artists of Hard Rock and was ranked as the 15th greatest live band by Hit Parader. Since its formation, Alice in Chains has released six studio albums, three EPs, three live albums, four compilations, two DVDs, 43 music videos, and 32 singles.

apple_music.editorial_notes: Original Alice in Chains vocalist Layne Staley shines in this powerful performance, which would be one of his last live appearances ever. His torn-up vocals are the passionate lifeblood of this acoustic set, fuelling the uneasy darkness of “Rooster” and delivering the lonesome howl that makes this rendition of “Down In a Hole” unforgettable. The band’s gloomy energy haunts throughout, but the skewed, dissonant grunge of the closing “The Killer Is Me” is especially mesmerising and harrowing.

lastfm.wiki_content: "MTV Unplugged" is a live album by the American rock band Alice in Chains, released on July 30, 1996, by Columbia Records. It was recorded on April 10, 1996, at the Brooklyn Academy of Music's Majestic Theatre for the television series "MTV Unplugged", in which musicians perform songs using acoustic instruments. The recording was the band's first concert since early 1994. During the intervening period, lead singer Layne Staley experienced problems with heroin addiction that prevented the band from performing live, and Alice in Chains temporarily ceased activity. The band resumed working together in 1995 and released its self-titled third studio album later that year, although it did not tour to promote the album. Despite Staley's health problems and guitarist Jerry Cantrell suffering from food poisoning, the performance was completed successfully. The set list primarily consisted of acoustic versions of previously released songs, along with brief tributes to Metallica and the debut performance of the new song "The Killer Is Me". The show was directed by Joe Perota and first aired on MTV on May 28, 1996. An acoustic version of "Over Now" was released as a single in July 1996, followed by "Would?" in October. Home video versions of the broadcast were released on VHS in October 1996 and on DVD in 1999. The album was reissued as a CD/DVD package with additional footage on September 18, 2007. The performance was Staley's final headlining appearance with Alice in Chains. He was hospitalised following a drug overdose several weeks before the release of "Unplugged" and subsequently ceased performing publicly. He died in 2002 following another drug overdose. "Unplugged" debuted at number three on the Billboard 200. Contemporary reviews were mixed, with some critics praising the acoustic arrangements of the band's heavier material while others considered the performances of songs that had previously appeared in acoustic form on "Sap" and "Jar of Flies" less distinctive. The album subsequently received greater critical recognition and was certified double platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). The home video release was also certified gold by the RIAA. Alice in Chains had not toured since co-headlining the Lollapalooza festival in mid-1993 and had not performed live since January 1994. The band had been scheduled to join Metallica's "Shit Hits the Sheds Tour" in July 1994, including an appearance at Woodstock '94, but cancelled its scheduled performances shortly before the tour began because of Staley's heroin addiction. Alice in Chains subsequently became inactive for approximately six months while its members pursued other projects. Staley joined the supergroup Mad Season and recorded its album "Above". Bassist Mike Inez appeared on Slash's solo album "It's Five O'Clock Somewhere", while Cantrell began developing material for a prospective solo album. Cantrell and drummer Sean Kinney also contributed to the Willie Nelson tribute album "Twisted Willie". Alice in Chains resumed working together in early 1995 and released its self-titled third studio album later that year. The band initially planned to tour in 1996 but ultimately abandoned those plans. During this period, MTV approached Alice in Chains about appearing on "MTV Unplugged". The band had previously declined several invitations to participate in the programme. Cantrell had expressed reservations about whether the group's heavier musical style would translate effectively to an acoustic performance, despite its previous acoustic releases "Sap" and "Jar of Flies". MTV producer Alex Coletti was more confident that Alice in Chains could adapt its music to the format. The "Unplugged" series had previously featured performances by other grunge bands, including Pearl Jam and Nirvana. After further discussions, Alice in Chains agreed to participate. Cantrell later stated that the band had waited until it felt sufficiently prepared to undertake the performance. The absence of an active concert tour also made the project easier to organise. Without other performance commitments, the band could concentrate its rehearsals on adapting its material to an acoustic setting. The acoustic format also had similarities to the band's earlier releases and to aspects of its self-titled album. Alice in Chains had limited experience performing acoustically in a live setting. In January 1994, the band had participated in an acoustic benefit concert for Fishbone bassist John Norwood Fisher. The performance represented a departure from the band's usual electric sound and received a mixed response from the audience. For the "Unplugged" performance, the band added guitarist Scott Olson of Heart to the lineup. Alice in Chains had previously collaborated with members of Heart, including vocalist Ann Wilson, who provided backing vocals on two songs on "Sap". One of those songs, "Brother", was included in the "Unplugged" set. Rehearsals took place in Seattle and were affected by difficulties with attendance and preparation. In early April 1996, the band travelled to New York to prepare for the recording. Producer Toby Wright, who had worked with Alice in Chains previously, returned to produce the "Unplugged" recording. The band rehearsed with Wright at Sony Music Studios. The Brooklyn Academy of Music's Majestic Theater, now known as the Harvey Theater, was selected as the venue. Its semicircular design was considered suitable for an acoustic performance. The stage was deliberately given an aged and distressed appearance to complement the atmosphere of the music. The production included artificial cracks and peeling paint, while candles were used as part of the lighting design. Lava lamps were also added shortly before the performance. Staley had recently dyed his hair pink, and the lighting design incorporated colours intended to complement the stage appearance and his hair. Different lighting schemes were prepared for individual songs. The concert took place on April 10, 1996. Cantrell was suffering from food poisoning after eating a hot dog before the performance and reportedly vomited repeatedly before going on stage. A waste bin was placed beside him during the performance. Staley also appeared to be in poor health, and his speaking voice between songs was noticeably weak. The band's guitar technician, Randy Biro, was also experiencing heroin withdrawal. According to Biro, Staley used heroin shortly before the performance. The musicians prepared thirteen songs for the concert, although some were discarded during rehearsals. The final set list included material from the band's releases up to that point, with the exception of its debut album, "Facelift". The band had considered performing "We Die Young" and "Love, Hate, Love", but omitted them because of time constraints. Cantrell played acoustic guitar and provided vocal harmonies with Staley, while Inez played acoustic bass and Kinney performed on drums. Olson joined Cantrell as a second guitarist. The performance opened with "Nutshell", followed by "Brother" and "No Excuses". The set subsequently included songs from "Dirt" and the self-titled album, including "Rooster", "Down in a Hole", "Would?", "Angry Chair" and "Heaven Beside You". "Got Me Wrong" from "Sap" was also performed. "Down in a Hole" was performed live for the first time during the concert. The recording process lasted more than three hours because of the setup required for cameras, lighting and sound, as well as repeated takes resulting from performance errors. "Sludge Factory" required several attempts, partly because Staley made mistakes with the lyrics. "Got Me Wrong" was attempted four times. The lyrics of "Sludge Factory" referenced Columbia Records president Don Ienner and Sony Music executive Michele Anthony, both of whom were present in the audience. After several unsuccessful attempts, the band eventually recorded a complete version. Members of Metallica were among the audience. During the performance, Inez played part of "Enter Sandman" before "Sludge Factory", while Cantrell began playing "Battery" before briefly performing "Gloom, Despair, and Agony on Me" from the television programme "Hee Haw". Inez's bass also contained a message directed at Metallica members who had recently cut their hair. The concert concluded with "The Killer Is Me", a song that Cantrell had begun writing more than a year earlier. Kinney suggested completing it for the performance, and Cantrell finished the song shortly before the concert. MTV provided the band with an initial version of the recording approximately two weeks after the concert. Staley objected to aspects of the footage, believing that some editing choices placed undue emphasis on his drug problems and portrayed him as being more impaired than he had been during the performance. Wright reviewed the footage and proposed changes to MTV, which were subsequently made. The final programme, directed by Joe Perota, aired on MTV on May 28, 1996. "Angry Chair", "Frogs" and "The Killer Is Me" were omitted from the television broadcast but were included on the physical releases of the performance. The album was announced shortly after the television broadcast and was initially scheduled for release on July 18, 1996. Its release was subsequently delayed until July 30. It was issued on CD and VHS. "Over Now" was released as a single on July 17, followed by "Would?" in October. A DVD release of the complete performance followed in 1999. The album was reissued in a CD/DVD package on September 18, 2007. The album received mixed reviews upon release. Stephen Thomas Erlewine of AllMusic considered that the performance added little to the band's existing albums and regarded some of the arrangements as less distinctive than the original recordings. Tom Sinclair of Entertainment Weekly found the acoustic arrangements ineffective in relation to the overall mood of the performance. Stephen Thompson of The A.V. Club similarly considered many of the reinterpretations predictable, although he viewed some performances of material from the self-titled album, particularly "Sludge Factory", more favourably. Robert Johnson of the San Antonio Express-News also criticised the lack of improvisation and compared the album unfavourably with Nirvana's "Unplugged" performance. Kevin O'Hare of The Republican considered the novelty of the "Unplugged" format to have diminished by the time Alice in Chains appeared, although he found the performance effective in places. Sandy Masuo of Rolling Stone praised the band's musicianship and its ability to perform effectively despite the difficulties surrounding the group, while stating a preference for its conventional electric sound. Select's Ben Mitchell praised performances of older material such as "Rooster" and "Brother" but was less positive about most of the selections from the self-titled album. Other contemporary critics were more favourable. Sara Sherr of the Philadelphia Inquirer highlighted the band's vulnerability and the humorous interactions during the performance. Steve Bailey of the Naples Daily News praised the vocal interplay between Cantrell and Staley and singled out "Rooster" and "Would?" as highlights. Chuck Klosterman of The Forum considered the stripped-down arrangements particularly effective and praised "Sludge Factory". Billboard critic Paul Verna described the album as an intimate and well-recorded performance and predicted that it would receive significant exposure on mainstream rock radio and MTV. The album subsequently gained greater recognition, particularly following Staley's death in 2002. Several publications later described the recording as a significant live album and highlighted Staley's performance in the context of his declining health. In 2016, Loudwire included the recording of "Down in a Hole" in a list of notable Staley performances. In 2017, Rolling Stone ranked Alice in Chains' "Unplugged" performance fourth on its list of the 15 best performances from the "Unplugged" series. For the album's 23rd anniversary in 2019, Metal Hammer described the performance as one of the strongest live albums associated with the programme. NME subsequently ranked the performance fifth on a list of the 20 best performances from the "Unplugged" series. Kinney later expressed satisfaction with the recording and considered it a strong conclusion to the band's period with Staley. Korn vocalist Jonathan Davis cited Alice in Chains' "Unplugged" performance as an influence on Korn's own appearance on the programme in 2007. In 2026, "Unplugged" was ranked 29th on Consequence's list of the 60 best albums of 1996. Read more on Last.fm. perplexity.description:
Alice In Chains’ MTV Unplugged captures the Seattle band at its most intimate and exposed. Recorded in April 1996 at Brooklyn Academy of Music’s Majestic Theatre and released by Columbia that July, the performance transforms songs such as “Down in a Hole,” “Rooster,” “No Excuses,” and “Nutshell” into stark acoustic arrangements built around Jerry Cantrell’s harmonies and Layne Staley’s haunting, vulnerable vocal presence. The stripped-down setting softens the band’s metallic force without diminishing its darkness, revealing the intricate songwriting beneath their grunge sound.

Initially met with a mixed critical response, the album has since become regarded as one of Alice In Chains’ defining achievements and a landmark of the MTV Unplugged series. It debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard 200 and was eventually certified double platinum in the United States, while the performance’s emotional weight has grown with time as a poignant document of Staley’s final headlining appearance. The 2026 Yellow Canary 30th Anniversary edition revisits this landmark live album in a commemorative reissue, preserving a pivotal chapter in the band’s history for a new generation of listeners.
